CUSTOMS AND FISHERIES PROTECTION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: AYLESWORTH moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 138) to amend the Customs, and Fisheries Protection Act. He said: This Bill proposes! to amend the Act so as to prescribe the method of proceeding where steps are taken to condemn a ship which has been seized and where such proceedings are taken, not in the Exchequer Court but in the Superior Court of a province. There is provision in the law as it stands that such proceedings may be taken either in the Exchequer Court or in the Superior Court of a province, but in some of the provinces no rules are irre-scribed for the taking of such proceedings in the provincial court and practical difficulty has resulted in endeavouring to get on. The proposal is to remove that difficulty by providing that, unless and until rules of procedure are prescribed by the provincial courts, the rules of procedure existing in the Exchequer Court shall be followed.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext: The long established practice of the government in this matter has been that the specie in the hands of the assistant receivers general is counted and checked by the inspectors from the Finance Department. House resumed the adjourned debate on the motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for the second reading of Bill (No. 95) respecting the naval service of Canada, the proposed amendment of Mr. Borden thereto, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Monk.

speakeroldname: Sir FREDERICK BORDEN (Minister of Militia and Defence).
speechtext:
In resuming the debate upon the motion for the second reading of the Bill to provide for a Canadian navy, I shall find it necessary to review, to some extent, a debate which took place in this House somewhat less than a year ago. In doing so I can hardly bring myself to believe that the opposition of to-day is composed of practically the same gentlemen who were in this House -and took part, some of them at any rate, in that debate in March, 1909. The hon. leader of the opposition and his deputy, the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), waxed eloquent in that important discussion; in fact the hon. member for North Toronto introduced a resolution, which was afterwards changed into the resolution which finally and unanimously passed this House. I did not observe that any one of the opposition dissented, not even my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk); he acquiesced, at any rate by his silence, in the terms of that resolution. It cannot be said

that the resolution was passed hastily. My hon. friend from North Toronto told us on that -occasion that he wrote out his resolution before he left Toronto, at any rate, that he placed it in the hands of the clerk on the very day this House met. My hon. friend did not move the resolution for some time afterwards, but I do not question in any way his motives, I am simply pointing out the fact that there was no hurry, no undue haste, that my hon. friend took all the time that he required before bringing the important matter to the attention of the House. Without detaining the House I shall proceed to read that resolution. It is as follows:
That all the words after ' that ' be struck out and the following substituted thereto:
This House fully recognizes the duty of the people of Canada, as they increase in numbers and wealth, to assume in larger measure the responsibilities of national defence.
The House i9 of opinion that under the present constitutional relations between the mother country and the self-governing dominions, the payment of regular and periodical contributions to the imperial treasury for naval and military purposes would not, so far as Canada is concerned, be the most satisfactory solution of the question of defence.
The House will cordially approve of any necessary expenditure designed to promote the speedy organization of a Canadian naval service in co-operation with and in close relation to the imperial navy, along the lines suggested by the admiralty at the last imperial conference, and in full sympathy with the view that the naval supremacy of Britain is essential to the security of commerce, the safety of the empire and the peace of the world.
The House expresses its firm conviction that whenever the need arises the Canadian people will be found ready and willing to make any sacrifice that is required to give to the imperial authorities the most loyal and hearty co-operation in every movement for the maintenance of the integrity and honour of the empire.
T may call attention to the fact that in this resolution there occurs the word 'speedy,' 'the speedy organizations of a Canadian naval service,' and that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) was the man who suggested that- some word of that kind should be introduced into the resolution. He has taken great credit, properly enough, for having done so in the speeches he has made in various portions of the Dominion and in the heart of the empire itself, in the city of London. Sir, can any one believe for a moment that the hon. gentlemen who lead the Conservative party to-day are the same gentlemen who moved, who acquiesced in, who took an active part in and boasted of the active part they had taken in the passing of that- resolution,
and who supported it in every sense for many months after the resolution was passed? But some change has come over the spirit of their dreams. It is difficult to understand what could have happened. We know that the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) took his vacation in the summer in England. There is an old saying that when the -cat is away the mice will play, and so it would appear that, the mice possibly played during the visit of my hon. friend to England in the summer, and they seemed to have played to some purpose, because I shall now read, and I wish to contrast with the one I have just read, the resolution which the leader of the -opposition moved here on February 3. It is as follows:
That all the words after the word ' that ' be left out and the following substituted therefor
The proposals of the government do uof follow the suggestions and recommendations of the admiralty, and in so far as they empower the government to withhold the naval forces of Canada from those of the empire in time of war are ill-advised and dangerous.
That no such proposals can safely be accepted unless they thoroughly ensure unity of organization and of action without which there can be no effective co-operation in any common scheme of empire defence.
That the said proposals while necessitating heavy outlay for construction and maintenance will give no immediate or effective aid to the empire and no adequate or satisfactory results to Canada.
That no permanent policy should be entered upon involving large future expenditures of this character until it has been submitted to the people -and has received their approval.
That in the meantime the immediate duty of Canada and the impending necessities of the empire can best be discharged and met by placing without delay at the disposal of the imperial authorities as a free and loyal contribution from the people of Canada such au amount as may be sufficient to purchase or construct two battleships or armoured cruisers of the latest Dreadnought type giving to the admiralty full discretion to expend the said su-m at such time and for such purposes of naval defence as in their judgment may best serve to increase the united strength of the empire and thus assure its peace and security.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. the leader of the opposition^ is apparently delighted at the reading of his resolution, much more so than he was at the reading of the resolution in the framing of which he was so proud to claim a part, and which was passed here in March, 1909. I propose to read shortly some of the arguments which were presented in 1909 in favour of the resolution then unanimously carried. I shall begin by reading an extract or two from the speech of the hon. the leader of the
No, no.
Yes.

He goes back on his policy and he proposes to tax the people of this country some $25,000,000 to send Dreadnoughts he knows not where, and to place them utterly beyond and outside of the control of the taxpayers of Canada. Now, Mr. Speaker, there is one more quotation from the hon. leader of the opposition.
Read it all.

It is not often that one has the extreme pleasure of I Sir FREDERICK BORDEN
being able to read quotations which are alike popular on both sides of the House and agreeable to all. My hon. friends opposite affect to enjoy these utterances of their leader, and I am sure my hon. friends on this side will be delighted to hear them, although we are sorry that the hon. gentleman has changed his mind. Let us hope that he may return some day to the sound opinions which he held in 1909. The hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) continued to say:
In so far as my right hon. friend the Prime Minister' to-day outlined the naval defence of this country I am entirely at one with him. I am entirely of opinion, in the first place, that the proper line upon which we should proceed in that regard is the line of having a Canadian naval force of our own. I entirely believe in that.
And yet he no longer believes in it, because he now proposes to take $25,000,000 out of the pockets of the people and send it away where the people of Canada will have no control over it. Then, the bon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) said:
The other experiment has been tried as between Australia and the mother country and it has not worked satisfactorily in every respect. In Great Britain the contribution has perhaps been regarded as rather unsatisfactory. In Australia it, in the end, failed to meet with the approval of the people for the reason that Great Britain felt constrained to ask Australia that the field of operations of the squadron should be extended to the China and Indian seas, and if the operations of that squadron were so extended the Australians felt that the contribution which they had been making for some years past was not really being used to give that protection to Australia which they felt it should have. So that, the policy of Australia at the present time is the policy of the submarine and torpedo boats which, in case of war, would cooperate with the armed cruisers and battleships of the British navy. It was pointed out in discussing this question that although the people of Australia provided a force of that kind they would provide a force which it would be very difficult if not impossible for Great Britain to send across the seas, and that when they were protecting themselves they were providing the best possible force for the protection of the empire.
Nine or ten months ago the hon. gentleman sympathized with Australia, which had found that to tax her people large sums of money for contribution or tribute for ships which would not be near the shores of Australia, but might be in the China seas, was no longer popular or proper. My hon. friend agreed with that view then; but to-day he wishes to tax the people of Canada $25,000,000 and to send it away out of sight of Canada where Canadians could have no possible interest in it. The hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) further said:

I am at one with the Prime Minister as far as that is concerned. Iam one with him in this respect also that I think that an expenditure of money designed for that purpose, as far as possible, ought, in the main at least, to be under the control of our own parliament and that by making an appropriation of that kind and attending to the defence of our own coasts, by co-operation and co-ordination with the imperial forces, we would be rendering a real service in the defence of the empire and we would be doing only our duty not only to Canada alone but to the empire as a whole.
It will be seen, therefore, that the hon. gentleman expressed himself as being in entire accord with the sentiments expressed by the Prime Minister, and so it will be instructive to see what were the sentiments of the Prime Minister with which the hon. the leader of the opposition was in absolute agreement as he said over and over again in his speech. Here is what the right hon. the Prime Minister said:
The empire of Britain has been founded less on war than on discovery and colonization, and wherever founded in any part of the world, whether by war or colonization or discovery, it has been maintained only by the free will and consent of the peoples who now acknowledge British supremacy. To-day the British empire is composed of a galaxy of young nations proud of their allegiance to the British Crown and proud also of their own independence. And though they may have a common aim, each has reserved to itself the duty and the right to develop its own resources and to attain its aim according to its own views, and by its own methods which may be best suited to the peculiar circumstances of each.
Mow, it may be said that defence which is the duty of all nations is a matter as to which there should be a common aspiration. Yes, I agree in that, but at the same time the young daughter nations of England have insisted that even in the matter of defence they should preserve in its entirety local autonomy, and that each should approach this subject according to its own lights. Let us not disguise the fact from ourselves that at present there is a passing wave in which we can trace anger, enthusiasm and fear, and which may be calculated by some to force us to depart from our policy and to contribute at once to the British navy. Well, Sir, let us view this question as it is, let us not blink at it, let us realize that it is not the way in which in the past we have understood our duty.
And the hon. the leader of the opposition acquiesced in every word of the statement of the right hon. the Prime Minister on. this line of his argument. The right hon. the Prime Minister continued:
This question is not new; we are familiar with it, it is not of to-day or of yesterday. I will not say it is as old as the hills, hut it is as old as confederation itself and it comes to the front periodically. It presented itself in a concrete form in the imperial conference of 1902 to those who were there assembled from all parts of the British empire conferring with the government of the mother country.
The proposition was placed before us that all the self-governing dominions of the British empire should contribute to the army and to the navy. The Canadian ministers who were present attending that conference did not view that project with any favour. They received it with respect but they declined to accept it and they presented their views in another form and they stated what they were prepared to do so far as Canada is concerned. Their views on that occasion were stated in a paper which has often been quoted in this House, but which I think it is opportune that I should quote to-day.
A paper 1 will not quote from, as it is very familiar-the	memorandum which
was placed in the hands of the conference of 1902 by the Canadian ministers. These are the sentiments, Mr. Speaker, which the leader of the opposition approved of in March, 1909. If they meant anything, they meant that the only self-respecting means by which Canada could in any way add to the responsibilities of defence which she was already bearing, was by the organization of a Canadian navy, but on lines which would enable it, if the people of Canada so desired, to co-operate with the great imperial navy.

Does my hon. friend mean to affirm that, from what my hon. friend the leader of the opposition said as to his agreement with the Prime Minister, that binds the leader of the opposition to an agreement with the memorandum placed before the imperial conference of 1902?

The right hon. the leader of the government stated that that memorandum had been before the people of Canada from 1902 down to that moment, and that no one on either side of the House had ever dissented from its terms.
The resolution of March Last undertook to carry out the plan of defence as defined by the imperi?' conference of 1907. That is what it said in very words.

I am afraid my hon. friend has not grasped the point which the hon. member for North Torontq was trying to make. The hon. member for North Toronto, as I understood him, asked me if I thought it was right to make the leader of the opposition responsible for that memorandum because it had been read by the Prime Minister, and because the leader of the opposition had approved of the Prime Minister's words in that regard; and I told my hon. friend from North Toronto, and I repeat it now, that that memorandum of 1902 has been before the people of this country for seven years, and has never been dissented from by any member of the opposition, nor by anybody in this country, so far as I know.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman would not think it unfair if I

called his attention to another part of my speech to which he has made no allusion.
While I venture to think that a system of torpedo boats and submarines such as has been adopted by the Commonwealth of Australia would be perhaps the most effective way in which we could assist Great Britain in a stated policy of naval defence, yet I agree that the Canadian government ought to have the advice of the British admiralty and lend itself to such co-operation and coordination as will be best for the whole empire.

I do not think the interruption was at all pertinent. The hon. gentleman was discussing the question of autonomy, and I did him the justice to read every word he said about it; and the beginning and end of his observations was that he approved of every word the right hon. leader of the government had said:
But, Mr. Speaker, there were other notable speeches made. The hon. member for North Toronto, during the vacation, after his leader had gone away, showed that he was still firm in the faith in a speech which he made at Halifax on the 25tli of August, 1909. In that speech-and I quote from the Halifax ' Herald,' which he will not dispute-he said:
This is the greatest step forward we have ever made iu Canada. We must be prepared to defend ourselves-
Not the British empire, but ourselves; it was Canada he was thinking about then. He forgot about it since.
-Canada lias a mighty future before her as a maritime power.
He was thinking about the future of Canada then, and he uttered some fine words and some splendid periods in regard to it. But to-day he and his party have become so dwarfed by this narrow policy which they have adopted that he sees nothing but blue ruin, Germany and hostile fleets, and nothing will avert that but the people of Canada putting their hands deep down in their pockets and taking out $25,000,000 and sending it away never to be seen again.
Nothing small about that.

The crisis had not arrived then; there was no emergency; everything was going on placidly and smoothly, and he could think of other things besides the danger of the German navy. Another remark of the hon. gentleman :
One effect of Canada's making a navy will be to give an impetus to steel shipbuilding in this country of ours, which will make immense employment and cause immense development in this country. One navy for the whole empire, though you may have several Mr. R, L. BORDEN.
fleets, one flag, one history iu the past, one grand mission.
The hon. leader of the opposition, at the Canada club banquet in London on Dominion day, said:
The establishment of a Canadian navy, upon which both parties were united, would serve a more practicable purpose than any such offer of Dreadnoughts.
And after he had returned and had heard of the capers which the mice had been performing in his absence, but still firm in the faith, he went to Halifax, where his deputy had been, and made a speech in October. He said:

That is forgotten. Nothing now but the policy of spending $25,000,000 for Dreadnoughts or ships to be sent to the other end of the world. Canadian commerce and trade routes and harbours are forgotten; under the overwhelming dread of the impending crisis. He said:

The House, while declaring its unalterable devotion to the British Crown-

from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), while the friends of the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) would be kept straight and right by the course that hon. gentleman was pursuing.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. I say that when the name of every other man who sits in this House to-day is forgotten, the name of Wilfrid Laurier will stand upon the annals, not only of Canada but of the empire, as that of a man who gave his life service for the best interests of his country, and through whose efforts a reconciliation and a better understanding of the duties of, at any rate, his friends, has been made, and to-day it would be impossible to stir up strife such as was frequently stirred up in the past.

May I ask a question? Will the hon. gentleman (Sir Frederick Borden), while he is on the subject, say whether or not he is in accord with the sentiments concerning independence expressed by the Prime Minister in 1892?

I du believe in bein' this Or that, ez it may happen One way or t'other hendiest is To ketch the people nappin';

This heth my faithful shepherd ben,
In pasture sweet heth led me,
An' this'll keep the people green To feed ez they hev fed me.
The resolution of the leader of the opposition, I presume, may fairly be considered to embody the policy of the opposition of to-day. The first paragraph of that resolution reads as follows:
The proposals of the government do not follow the suggestions and recommendations of the admiralty, and, in so far as they empower the government to withhold the naval forces of Canada from those of the empire in time of war, are ill-advised and dangerous.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) says that we have not followed the proposals of the admiralty, and he spent a good deal of time in endeavouring to enforce that proposition. I have not been able to discover in his remarks, which I have carefully read, anything in the shape of argument. A good deal was said about Australia, and we were told, and the country was given to understand-for, I suppose the speech was made largely for the country- that, while Australia and New Zealand had done everything that daughter-nations of the mother country ought to do and had followed obediently the direction of the admiralty, we Canadians had failed to do so. Well, now, take the case of Australia. One of the great difficulties which my hon. friend the leader of the opposition sees in our policy-or claims to see, for I do not understand how he can see it-is that we do not automatically place the control of our navy under the British admiralty. Is that the objection?

If the hon. gentleman desires to know what the point I made was, I can tell him in a few words. I say that the resolution of March, 1909, declared expressly and explicitly that any naval service to be established should be in accordance with the suggestions made by the admiralty in 1907, and I read-as the hon. gentleman will find at page 3061 of ' Hansard '

the words of Lord Tweedmouth, the First Lord of the Admiralty, in which he expressly declared that command must be reserved to the admiralty of all such forces.

And nobody objects to that. When any Canadian fleet or any Australian fleet is serving with Sir FREDERICK BOBDEN.
the British navy, of course it will be under the command of the senior officer of the British navy. That is one thing. But it is quite another thing to say that, the Canadian fleet shall automatically serve whenever war is declared. The Canadian Bill reserves the right to the Governor in Council
Who would have command in that case?

In that
case, I suppose, the command would remain as it was.
It is for that reason that I say it does noi follow the suggestions of the admiralty.

The admiralty lias never suggested that the fleet of one of the Dominions shall pass automatically under the control of the admiralty. It remained for the super-loyal opposition in Canada to make the suggestion, for nobody else ever thought of such a thing. Let me prove that. But, first, my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) says that he read from Lord Tweedmouth. I know he did, and it was not very much in point. If there was any point to it at all, we were directed to follow the lines laid down in the conference of 1907, which were that we should build the smallest class of cruisers, and not even as large ships as we are building now, no large cruiser or battleship was ever thought of. But Lord Tweedmouth said other things which my hon. friend did not read. I did not intend to read this, but I have it here. He said:
Gentlemen, what I have to say is that the admiralty and His Majesty's government are perfectly ready to meet these contributors to admiralty funds in a liberal and conciliatory manner.
Speaking of Australia and New Zealand :
We do not wish to insist that the contributions from the colonies should necessarily be in the form of money only. We ate quite ready to enter into any arrangement with the colonies that may seem most suitable to them, and which may seem to bring advantage to the navy and advantage to the colonies themselves.
He was thinking of the colonies, something which the new tangled policy of the opposition does not think of:
I have here a short statement of what may be called the general principle on which the admiralty desires to meet the representatives of the self-governing dominions of the King beyond the seas.
Then he goes on:
In the opinion of the government, while the distribution of the fleet must be determined by strategical requirements of which the admiralty are the judge, it would be of great

assistance if the colonial governments would undertake to provide for local service in the imperial squadrons the smaller vessels that are useful for defence against possible raids, or for co-operation with a squadron, and also to . equip and maintain docks and lifting establishments which can be used by His Majesty's ships. ... I understand, that in Australia particularly, and in South Africa, it is desired to start some naval service of your own. Perhaps I might suggest that if the provision of the smaller craft which are necessarily incident to the work of a great fleet of modern battleships could be made locally, it would be a very great help to the general work of the navy.
What navy? The British navy. That provision should be made locally, and in time of stress and emergency in the quarter in which those ships are, they could be of immense assistance to the British navy.
You cannot take the small craft such as torpedo boats and submarines across the ocean, and for war ships to arrive in South Africa, or in Australia, or in New Zealand, or in Canada, and find ready to their hand well trained men in good vessels of this kind, would be an enormous advantage to them.
Are we not following the directions of the admiralty as proposed in 1907? It seems to me we are.
There is, I think, the further advantage in these small flotillas, that they will be an admirable means of coast defence

We- have coasts on both oceans which require defence. The British fleet has been withdrawn from Halifax and Esquimau and we propose to take its place with small vessels which the British admiralty kept at those two places, by a navy of our own, and in that way to relieve the mother country of further responsibility for our own local defence.
-that you will be able by the use of them to avoid practically all danger from any sudden raid which might be made by a cruising squadron.
Is that not of some use? A word now about Australia. I do not care to make comparisons, but comparisons unfavourable to Canada have been made over and over again in this debate, comparisons and inferences which are entirely unfounded. Now I asked the other day from the Department of Marine and Fisheries some information as to what was understood in Australia with reference to bringing their ships automatically or otherwise under the control of the admiralty, and I find the following facts. In the proceedings of the imperial conference and the Imperial Parliamentary Sessional Papers, 19th August, 1909, paragraph 3 says, after stating that the commonwealth government have exclusive control in time of peace, and while on the Australian station:

Further, when placed by the Commonwealth government at the disposal of the admiralty in war time, the vessels should be under the control of the naval commander-in-chief

Mark the words:

when placed by the Commonwealth government.
Nothing automatical about that. I find in the Australia Defence Act, read first in September, 1908, cited as; the Defence Act, 1906:
In time of war, the Governor General may

The very words used in our own Act.
-subject to the provisions of this Act, place the defence force or any part thereof under the orders of the commander of any portion of the King's regular forces, or the King's regular naval forces, as the case may be.
But note in the interpretation clause of this Act what war means:
Any invasion or apprehended invasion, or attack or apprehended attack on the Commonwealth or any territory under the control of the Commonwealth, by any enemy or armed force.
That is the law of Australia, and if my hon. friend -had looked up the law he would have saved himself a great deal of trouble.
May I ask the hon. gentleman whether the Act he has read just now provides in any way for a navy, whether it is not merely an Act for a naval militia?
No, it is the Defence Act of Australia, which includes both the military and the navy.

The hon. gentleman has not answered my question. I asked if that Act from which he has quoted provides in any way for a navy. I know it provides for a naval militia, I know it provides for a military militia, and I know too, that it does not provide for a navy.

I have no doubt about it. Of course I do not want to speak too positively, but this is the information which I have, and which was prepared for me by the naval experts of the Marine and Fisheries office. Now what about an emergency?
In time of war or emergency, or upon a declaration by the senior naval officer representing the British government, that a condition of emergency exists, all the vessels of the naval force of the Commonwealth shall be placed by the Commonwealth government under the orders of Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty.
Paragraph 9, says:
It is, however, to be understood-

This is not the law, this is only a memorandum.
-It is, however, to be understood that if any of the coast defence vessels be desired in seas remote from Australia, the approval of the Commonwealth government shall first be obtained to their removal.
But I was not satisfied with all this and so having learned that Admiral Kingsmill had a code with the authorities in Australia, I asked the admiral to send this message:
February 5, 1910.
Captain in charge,
Sydney, Australia.
l'lease inform me by telegraph as soon as possible whether, in the event of war, vessels of Australian navy pass automatically without any action under control of admimalty.
(Sgd.) KINGSMILL.
The answer came on February 8 as follows:
Kingsmill, Ottawa.
With reference to your telegram, transfer control to the admiralty is not to be automatic but subject to approval of Commonwealth government on declaration of war.
Perhaps that may possibly satisfy my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) that this first paragraph of his resolution was quite unnecessary, and that the deductions suggested by it are absolutely unfounded.
What evidence is there that there was any difference of opinion between the gentlemen who were sent to the conference to represent Canada and the admiralty, or any representative of the admiralty participating in that conference. At any rate, Mr. Speaker, Canada boasts of independence, of autonomy of nationhood. Surely when she solemnly sends a deputation to the mother country on the invitation of the mother country to take part in a conference, she is not to go there with her ears and mouth closed. They wanted consultation and they had the opportunity of consultation; we wanted advice, they wanted to know what the conditions were, their statesmen, admirals, men anxious to do the thing which would be the best for Canada, and the best for the empire. But taking the lowest point of view and looking carefully at every word in this blue-book, there is not a single word there to indicate that there was any difference of opinion whatever between the members of the British government or the representatives of the admiralty, and the Hon. Mr. Brodeur and myself. What did Mr. Asquith, the premier of England, say in the statement which he read to the House of Commons? On August 26 he said:
The conference, which has just concluded its labours, was convened under the terms of resolution 1 of the conference of 1907. In Sir FREDERICK BORDEN
the invitation sent by His Majesty's government at the end of April to the governments of the dominions, it was stated that the object of the conference would be to discuss the general question of naval and military defence of the empire, with special reference to recent proposals from New Zealand and Australia, and to the resolution passed on the 29th March, by the House of Commons of the Dominion of Canada. It was further stated that the conference would be of a purely consultative character and that it would be held in private. It follows that all resolutions come to and proposals approved by the conference which has now been held, must be taken, so far as the delegates of the dominions are concerned, to be ad referendum, and of no binding force unless and until submitted to their various parliaments.

It speaks there of certain resolutions come to, and proposals accepted and to be referred to parliament. Were not certain resolutions accepted, and if so why have they not been brought down to parliament?

No, there was no resolution at all. It was found at the second meeting of the conference in reference to naval matters that an agreement was impossible as to a line of policy in which all of the dominions could agree. New Zealand, as will appear from the papers, declared her unwillingness to agree to a policy of building up a navy of her own. She was determined to adhere to the plan of an annual contribution. So soon as that fact was ascertained, it was agreed that each one of the dominions should meet with the First Lord of the Admiralty and his_ advisers, to arrange each by itself the policy it would follow, and that is what was done, and every resolution and every decision that was reached is recorded in thi3 Canadian blue-book.
To resume the reading of Mr. Asquith's official statement:
I should add in special reference to the delegates from South Africa that they did not feel themselves in a position, in regard to either naval or military defence, to submit or to approve positive proposals until the union of South Africa was an accomplished fact.
With this preface I will briefly summarize the main conclusions of the conference in regard, first to military, and next to naval defence.
I.shall read the conclusions as to military defence, because I think they throw a distinct light upon the general policy of defence, which has been adopted by the mother country and by the colonies.
Military defence. After the main conference at the foreign office, a military conference took place at the war office, and resulted in an agreement on the fundamental principles set out in papers which had been prepared by the general staff for consideration by the delegates.
The substance of these papers (which will

be included among the papers to be published) was a recommendation that, without impairing the complete control of the government of each Dominion over the military forces raised with it,

In a real emergency, not in a fancied one.
-in a real emergency, their forces could be rapidly combined into one homogeneous imperial army.
Naval Defence.
Naval defence was discussed at meetings of the conference held at the Foreign Office on the 3rd, 5th, and 6th August. The admiralty memorandum which had been circulated to the Dominion representatives formed the basis of the preliminary conference.
The alternative methods which might be adopted by the Dominion governments, in cooperating in imperial naval defence were discussed. New Zealand preferred to adhere to her present policy of contribution; Canada and Australia preferred to lay the foundation of fleets of their own.
To lay the foundation of fleets of their own, mark that:
It was recognized that in building up a fleet a number of conditions should be conformed to. The fleet must be of a certain size, in order to offer a permanent career to the officers and men engaged in the service. The personnel should be trained and disciplined under regulations similar to those established in the Royal Navy,

And that is the intention with reference to the Canadian fleet, as the Bill itself will show:
-in order to allow of both interchange and union between the British and the Dominion services; and with the same object, the standard of vessels and armaments should be uniform.
A remodelling of the squadrons maintained in far eastern waters was considered on the basis of establishing a Pacific fleet, to consist of three units in the East Indies, Australia and China seas, each comprising, with some variations, a large armoured cruiser of the new ' Indomitable ' type, three second-class cruisers of the ' Bristol ' type, six destroyers of the ' River ' class, and three submarine of ' C ' class.
The generous offer, first of New Zealand and then of the Commonwealth government, to contribute to imperial naval defence by the gift each of a battleship was accepted with the substitution of cruisers of tne new ' Indomitable * type for battleships-these two ships to be maintained, one on the China and one on the Australian station.
Now, in the debate on the resolution which was passed here in Mnrch, 1909, there was not a suggestion from any of these gentlemen opposite.
Yes, there was.

No, Sir; it was not suggested that we should at that moment do anything more than we did, and there is nothing in the resolution except to take the power, at any time in the future, to give if we saw fit. But there was not a word spoken to indicate that it was in the mind of any of my hon. friends opposite that it was our duty at that time to give one dollar towards a Dreadnought for the British navy.
Separate meetings took place at the admiralty with the representatives of Canada, Australia and New Zealand, and general statements were agreed to in each case for further consideration by their respective governments.
We had no power to settle anything. We followed, so far as we could, what we thought were the instructions contained in the resolution unanimously passed by this House. That is what we did. We stated frankly to the conference that we had no power whatever to go beyond the policy iaid down there.
As regards Australia, the suggested arrangement is that with some temporary assistance from imperial funds the Commonwealth government should provide and maintain the Australian unit of the Pacific fleet.
The contribution of the New Zealand gov-
There is no provision to that effect.
It is left to the Governor in Council.
Left entirely open?

But the navy is to be organized on the lines of the 'British service, and common -sense, if there were no other motive, would naturally cause the government to provide the same number of years. The British navy has had the experience of hundreds of years, and it contains the best organized fleet of any navy in the world to-day
Hear, hear.

And no government of any British dominion would be so foolish as to organize its fleet upon any other lines. With regard to the third resolution, we are told that there is heavy outlay and no results:

Such proposals, while necessitating heavy outlay for protection and maintenance, would give no immediate or effective aid to the empire and no adequate or satisfactory results to Canada.
And in order to get results to Canada, my hon. friend proposes that we should vote $25,000,000 of money and hand that money over to the British admiralty. Well, it does not seem to me that such a policy would bring about results of any great consequence to Canada. Canada can afford to do it if she likes, but what the hon. gentlemen wanted, as I have proved by quotations from their speeches ten short months ago, was speedy action towards the organization of a navy. But it takes something besides ships to make a navy. The most important is the personnel, and we have none of that to-day in Canada. Men and officers are required to make a navy. The machine, as compared with the man, is a small matter, and can always be got. But educated seamen are the work of years. My hon. friend has reminded us of that and he proposes to get over the difficulty by putting off the day and marking time. In fact, the policy of the Conservative party seems to be: Two ' Dreadnoughts ' and mark time.
My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) in March last objected very strongly to any contribution. This is what he said:
The first and greatest objection which I have to a fixed money contribution is that it bears the aspect of hiring somebody else to do what we ourselves ought to do; as though a man, the father of a family, in lusty health and strength, should pay his neighbour something per month for looking after the welfare and safety of his home instead of doing that duty himself. That seems to me, when you work it out, to be a basic objection to this form of aid. It goes still further than that. Suppose you contribute this year your sum, and next year your equal sum, and thereafter year after year. After ten or twelve, or twenty, or thirty years, you will have paid out an immense amount of money. You will have been protected m the meantime; but in Canada itself there will be no roots struck, there will be no residue left, there will be no preparation of the soil, or beginning of the growth of the product of defence. Yet some time or other, no one can doubt that with resources and with a population constantly increasing, we must and will have in this country a naval force of our own for our coast and home defence.
And yet, to-day, ten months later, the hon. gentleman wishes to put it off indefinitely and to get rid of all this responsibility by giving $25,000,000 to hire somebody else to do that which he admitted ten months ago was the first duty of this country.
And, going on, he says:
The second policy to which I would refer is the assuming by ourselves of the defence of our own ports and coasts, in constant and free

co-operation with the imperial forces of the mother country. Let us see what are the objections to and what may be urged in support of that second policy. It has its advocates and its opponents. In the first place we begin with no plant, no expert skill, no trained cadets, no trained sailors. In those respects, Canada is a blank sheet. Whatever may be necessary has to be collected and assembled and developed with such expedition and in such abundance as circumstances will allow. Under that system our first vessels would be .British built, British equipped, British manned, British officered from stoker to captain. There is no other way in which we could proceed.
I hope we have found a better way
We are absolutely bare of the skill, the experience, the training and the machinery necessary to put one single war vessel on a proper footing; but-and it is but the begin-ning^of a circle-the first Canadian owned vessel, built and equipped in Britain, and sent out to defend our coasts would become the nucleus and the training ground of Canadian stokers, Canadian sailors, and Canadian officers, and by and by perhaps, of a Canadian admiral on the Canadian coast. Those were splendid words; that was a splendid policy. My hon. friend had taken days and weeks to think that out and it does him credit. But what shall be said of him now that, within ten months, he absolutely turns his back upon that splendidly-outlined policy?

Yes.

Will they be manned, and so forth, in four years?
How many of these vessels do you propose to put on the Pacific coast?
There will be two ' Bristols ' on the Pacific coast, two of the eleven ships, and t-wo ' Bristols ' on the Atlantic coast.
These two ships that are to be stationed on the Pacific, are they to he used when a strike occurs, as mentioned by the Prime Minister the other day?
Well, really, if the hon. gentleman thinks that is quite consonant with his dignity as a member of parliament, I must say I do not.
What is the tonnage of the 'Rainbow'?

3,600 tons. Now I will read a few extracts from what Admiral Kingsmill has said:
Taking into consideration the matter of training, the importance of commencing at once, also the fact that building the vessels in Canada would necessitate a training ship for some time, I laid before Mr. Brodeur a memorandum as to the advisability of obtaining, if possible, a larger ship.
I have already stated that the 'Niobe' was suggested, and negotiations are now proceeding with reference to the purchase of that ship. That ship has been recommended strongly by the admiralty.
What is the age of the vessel?
Ten years.
What is her gun power?
About 16 guns.
What kind of guns?
16 6-inch guns. She is a ship of 11,500 tons. Her speed is about 20 knots.
What is she to cost?

$1,075,000. Now as to the Bristol cruisers:
They would fill an important duty in warding off attacks against commerce or against the coasts of Canada of any enemy's raiding cruisers, and would also act as commerce destroyers. Their first duty is to seek out and destroy the enemy's destroyers. It is most imperative for a battle fleet cruising to know, when night comes on, that the ground they have to go over has been cleared of the enemy's destroyers. ... In the event of a British fleet coming over, these cruisers would have gleaned information of the movements of an enemy's fleet, and so act as an advanced screen after which they could join up with the British fleet.
How many knots an hour can these ships make?
The Bristol 25 knots and the destroyers 27 knots.
The minister has not given the gun power of the Bristol.

These vessels are of the newest type and the details of their gun power are not published; it is not considered desirable to publish them. I think it will be evident from what I have said that the ships which have been selected for us by the British admiralty are ships of the latest type, and that the arrangement which has been made with reference to the fleet unit adopted for Canada is of a kind which takes cognizance of the geographical position of this country, and the fact that we have two large oceans separated by a distance of some 4,000 miles, the idea being, and it is the only ideal that would be considered by the people of Canada, that we should begin at one and; the same time the development of our navy on the Pacific and on the Atlantic. I may say that it did not appeal to Mr. Brodeur and myself as being desirable or at all in accordance with the views or wdth the ambitions of the people of the whole of Canada that we should place one unit upon one of the oceans; we held it was much better to begin more gradually, to begin to develop the personnel, which as I have said, is the very foundation of a navy, and to do it upon both of the great coasts of Canada, and later on it will be open to whatever government is in power in Canada to take such course as it may see fit as to the future development of the Canadian navy.
How would the minister provide for an* emergency in the meantime?

We are
quite satisfied with the provision which is now made for an emergency.
I ask mv hon. friend how long this naval service would take to equip and make effective?
I quoted what the Prime Minister said.
Has the minister any proposal to make in regard to providing for an emergency in the meantime?
Our friends of the opposition are doing that.
Then I have to ask my hon. friend if the proposals of the opposition are satisfactory to him?

I am not aware that the members of this side of the House have treated any of the opposition

speakers, particularly leading members of the opposition, in this way. I can stand any amount of heckling or nonsense, but I did not come here for that purpose to-day, and I think perhaps I might be allowed to get through with my statement and allow somebody else to follow.
I must beg the hon. minister's pardon; I had no desire whatever to embarrass him in his speech. I asked him a question and had it not been for his answer nothing further would have been said.
I think the question he put as to an emergency is not a proper question to interject.
I can understand that if the minister did not want to answer it.

Now with regard to the cost, I have two statements here which I shall not read in detail, but I think it is perhaps desirable that a few words should be given on this point. 1 have here a paper prepared by Admiral Kingsmill from which it appears that the cost, exclusive of construction, would be for the first four years as follows: For the first year, $1,250,000; for the second year. $1,247,000; for the third year, $1,704,000; for the fourth year, $2,250,000. It does not allow for any of the ships proposed in the government programme being completed in the four years. Should any of them be completed and commissioned within this period, account would have to be taken of their upkeep.
As I understand these sums do not include anything for the upkeep of the proposed new vessels.
No. I have also a statement of the estimated annual cost of maintenance, when the ships are completed, commissioned and fitted out. This estimate, including $100,000 for contingencies, is $3,680,000.
Does that take into account interest and depreciation?
No.

My hon. friend has referred to the memorandum of Admiral Kingsmill. Would it be convenient, if it is too long to read, for my hon. friend to hand it in to ' Hansard ' so that we could get the entire memorandum?
I will see whether that can be done.
As my hon. friend has quoted from it I suppose it is right to have it put on 'Hansard'.

What happened was that Admiral Kingsmill gave me data and I took them down, so it wa3 perhaps scarcely correct to say it was Admiral Kingsmill's memorandum but I think I can hand it in; I shall endeavour to do so.

It seems to be a memorandum connected with this matter, and as it is probably lengthy we can claim that it should be laid on the table of the House. I think it would be a convenient way for the minister to hand it in to 'Hansard', otherwise I would insist on my right to see the memorandum itself.
There is no objection to the hon. gentleman seeing it. It is chiefly notes which I have made.

Will my hon. friend lay it
on the table?
Well, I will see.
1 think that document is necessary for our information, my hon. friend has referred to it.
There is no objection, but I would not like to hand it in immediately until I have looked it over.

My hon. friend must really excuse me. This is a question of order and I would like my hon. friend to let me know before he has 'finished his remarks if he intends to give us communication of that memorandum.

The memorandum which I hold in my hand from which I gave a few extracts is a memorandum prepared bv the Admiral and which I intend to place on the pages of 'Hansard'. I have given the annual expenditure for the first four years, the estimated cost of maintenance after the ships are in hand and completed.

I would call _ the hon. gentleman's attention-because it is important-to the estimated cost given by the Prime Minister on authority, when he moved the second reading of the Bill. He makes the annual cost, after the construction is done, and the work going on, at four

and a quarter million dollars. There is a large disparity between the two.

Now, with regard to the cost of construction. The cost of construction is at British prices. Of course the prices I have been giving for victualling and up-keep and all that are at Canadian rates, but the estimate of construction is at British rates, and that should be understood. I am not in a position to say how much more the ships will cost if built in Canada, but they certainly will cost more. I think, from a Canadian standpoint-as had been pointed out by so many hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House-it would be very desirable, if possible, that they should be constructed in Canada, if the excess of price involved is not too great. That can only be ascertained by asking for tenders, which of course will be done. It appears that the ships would cost $11,015,000, substituting the ' Niobe ' for the ' Boadicea,' which appears in this memorandum as costing $1,750,000. The ' Niobe ' is to be a training ship, and is to be procured very shortly, and she will cost $1,075,000. The difference of $675,000 between the cost of the ' Boadicea5 and ' Niobe ' will reduce the estimate, which is $11,690,000 to $11,015,000. Then there are estimates for the construction of a naval college, furnishing the same, workshops, two houses, barracks, &c.-I need not read the items, amounting to $715,000.
Canadian figures?

Yes. The $715,000 would be Canadian figures. It is for the construction of buildings to spread over several years. The total cost of construction, therefore, would be of ships and buildings, $11,730,000, about $11,000,000 of which is estimated at British prices.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I had intended to say a single word as to the annual cost. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) referred to the inauguration of what he called the era of militarism, and he thought that this expenditure would be sure to run up from year to year as our military expenditure had, and he believed that eventually the tax would be very high. Now, the military expenditure of Canada amounts to about 80 cents per head of the present population, and I take it that when construction is completed, the naval expenditure combined with the expenditure on militia would not amount to more than $1.25 per head of the present population of Canada, and I believe that the annual increase of population will keep the figure at about that per capita rate. It does not seem to me that for a country like Canada, rich and prosperous and rapidly becoming great, an expenditure of $1.25 per head for its total cost for defence would be a very high rate. Ij therefore, think my hon. friend from East Grey may possess his soul in patience and need not worry over the expenditure.

Is it not a fact that since the militia was reorganized the expendi-Sir FREDERICK BORDEN.
ture has increased to $6,500,000 per annum, when it was formerly only $2,500,000? That being so, may we not reasonably expect a somewhat proportionate increase in the naval expenditure?

I do not think so. The hon. gentleman stated the other night, and he stated correctly, that the expenditure on militia had increased, but he did not state that a very large part of that increased expenditure was due to taking over the garrisons of Halifax and Esquimalt and to increasing the permanent force of 800 or 900 men up to practically
3,000.	That accounts for a large part of the increase in the militia expenditure, and I am sure the hon. gentleman does not object to our relieving the British taxpayer to that extent.
What I did object to, was that while in 1896 the officers and those who controlled the force cost the country $16,000, the men who do the same work to-day cost us $73,000.

I am not going to be turned aside now to deal with that question, because I have stated over and over again the reasons for that, and I have laid on the table of the House a memorandum from Major Genaral Sir Percy Lake explaining fully every dollar of the increase.
Does the minister object to my endeavouring to get a clear understanding as to that matter?

I think I might be allowed to finish my remarks. I have never known a similar case of interruption in my parliamentary experience of thirty-six years. When a minister is attempting to make a statement upon an important subject, whether his statement is acceptable or not, it is usually listened to. With regard to the per capita charge I shall say no more. The hon. gentleman, in, the fourth part of his resolution, says:
That no permanent policy should be entered upon involving large future expenditure of this character until it has been submitted to the people and has received their approval.
This is rather an astounding proposition, Mr. Speaker, after what took place ten months ago. Parliament was then fresh from the people. The hon. member from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) scarcely waited until the ink was dry upon the returns of the elections before he took up the question of considering and bringing before parliament our duty in the matter of providing for naval defence. It was seriously considered, and a certain line of policy was unanimously agreed to. At that time the question that there was any duty devolving upon us to go to the country on
33.33

this subject was never raised by anybody.
I will venture to say that no such misconstruction of responsible government was ever heard of in the British parliament or ever before suggested in this parliament. The people sent us here for the purpose of dealing with all important public questions. Is it to be said that every time an important question comes up, we shall go back to the people, particularly after parliament has unanimously agreed to a certain line of policy? Who would think of putting forward such a monstrous proposition as that? I think the hon. gentleman surely cannot be serious. I am reminded that the hon. gentlemen themselves suggested the addition to the resolution of March last, of the words to the effect that we should not wait, but get to work on a navy at once; and I have read extracts from the hon. gentlemen's speeches to prove that they were the most enthusiastic advocates of the immediate construction and organization of a navy. Yet we are told to-day that we should go back to the people. But I do not observe that the hon. gentleman thinks it at all necessary to go to the people for their approval of the proposal to tax them to the extent of $25,000,000 to buy two Dreadnoughts. Why, Mr Speaker, everybody knows that the Militia Act of Canada for the last fifty years, and I dare say ever since Canada has had responsible government, has made provision-and it is there to-day-for the organization of a militia navy. So this is no new policy. It is there authorized by the people; and it has always been perfectly understood that Canada had there the authority at any moment she felt financially able to undertake the additional responsibility of naval defence.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

I wish simply to add to what I have said with reference to the remarks of the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) that I observe he is opposed to military expenditure or defence expenditure of all kinds. A3 I understand him he is against militarism, and seems to think that any expenditure of the kind is to be classed under that head I can understand therefore why my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) should support this resolution. The other evening he said that he favoured our expending $25,000,000 on Dreadnoughts, and doing nothing else, because possibly that would be all the expenditure necessary. In his view, that would be a happy way of escaping from all future expenditure because perhaps another call would not be made on us for at least a generation or
twenty years. Therefore it was from motives of economy that my hon. friend supports the resolution of the leader of the opposition. The gift of $25,000,000 might be a cheap way of getting put of our obligations because we might never have to put up any more, and in any case there would not likely be another call for the next twenty years.
The last part of the resolution of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition reads as follows: -
That in the meantime

That is before the creation of a navy was submitted to the consideration of the people

-that in the meantime the immediate duty of Canada and the impending necessities of the empire can best he discharged and met by placing without delay at the disposition of the imperial authorities, as a free and loyal contribution from the people of Canada, such an amount as may be sufficient to purchase or construct two battleships or armoured cruisers of the latest Dreadnought type, giving to the admiralty full discretion to expend such sum at such time and for such purposes on naval defence as, in their judgment, may best serve to increase the united strength of the empire and thus insure its peace and security.
So that it is not necessarily Dreadnoughts which the hon. gentleman advocates-it is anything on which the British government may choose to expend money for the British navy. My hon. friend and his supporters based this resolution upon the idea that a crisis or an emergency exists. Otherwise there is no ground or excuse for putting such a proposal before this House. Because there is an emergency, the hon. gentleman proposes that we shall hand over $25,000,000 as a present to the British admiralty to buy two Dreadnoughts or anything else they might see fit in the way of naval defence. But when did this crisis or emergency arise? I have pointed out that in the mind of the hon. gentleman and of his lieutenant, the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) there was_ no crisis or emergency in March last. I have read the speech of the leader of the opposition delivered in London in July last, from which it would appear that, in his opinion, there was no crisis then. Wa3 it because my hon. friend had been looking at that magnificent array of battleships in the Thames which he spoke about so eloquently here a few weeks ago, that his mind was then kept in the due equipoee which it enjoyed in March last? Was it on that account that he did not see any crisis then although he was in London, the very heart of the empire, where it might be supposed to be found if it existed anywhere. On the contrary, the hon. gentleman then said he was for a Canadian navy and against a contribution of Dread-

noughts. Was it in August? Certainly not. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) told us, as late as August last in Halifax, that the proper policy was the building of a Canadian navy. There was no indication then of any impending danger. Neither was it in October, because in Toronto both these hon. gentlemen assured the people that they were still strong in the belief that a Canadian navy was the proper thing. It was certainly not in November, because we had the same assurances then. Nor'was it in December because in the city of Montreal I had the honour of listening to my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, making a strong and effective speech in favour of the adoption of a Canadian policy and the creation of a Canadian navy. When then did it come and whence did it come? As I have said, it showed its first symptoms on the 12th of January last when my hon. friend indicated that there were in his mind some germs which indicated a coming attack of blue funk-shall I say?-or the dread of some impending crisis. We have in England in the navy what has been known a long time as the blue sea school, and I have observed during the recent elections there that somebody has said that another school has taken its rise in England, and that is the blue funk school. The threat of German invasion was used, as we know, during the recent elections in England.
Well, Sir, the hon. gentleman has seen fit to launch hi? policy. That policy is, to give the admiralty of the mother country a sum of money sufficient to buy two Dreadnoughts. Now, what does that policy involve? It certainly involves delay in the matter, of proceeding with the real work of beginning, constructing and organizing a Canadian navy to co-operate, when required, with the British navy. But more than that is involved. As I have pointed out, it involves a heavy expenditure without any direct benefit whatever to Canada in the way of building up a navy. We are a people of seven and a half millions. Years ago we undertook the defence of this country on land. Everybody agreed ten months ago that the time had arrived when we should undertake that defence upon the waters adjacent to bur country. But this proposition of hon. gentlemen opposite means a begging of the question, it means expending $25,000,000 without contributing in any way whatever-as to personnel, as to shipbuilding, as to docks or anything else which is important-to building up a navy or educating the people of Canada towards co-operation with the mother country in our own defence.
Now, I ask your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, for a few moments while I read some authorities upon this question of whether or not there is an emergency. It seems to Sir FREDERICK BORDEN.
me to be a very important question. For, if there is not an emergency, then my hon. friend's resolution is not to the point. And I think I can show without very great difficulty that there is no emergency. This is a serious question and one which we should approach seriously. We should make the effort by every means in our power to inform ourselves with reference to this question. I propose first to read briefly from a statement of Sir William White, who is ex-constructor of the British navy, a man who might be presumed to have very considerable knowledge as to the power of the British navy itself and as to the strength and character of the other navies of the world. Sir William White said:
German activity in warship building attracts most attention for the moment and there is a tendency to treat existing conditions as if they were unprecedented. Every one familiar with the events of the last half century (since the iron-clad area began), knows that this is not true. That period has been marked by a succession of struggles for supremacy in sea power, and more critical situations have occurred in the past than that which now exists. From 1857 to 1870 France was a formidable competitor; indeed, for the first ten years of that period, her war fleet was stronger, relatively to the British navy, than any single power has been since. The combined strength of French and Russian fleets furnished the standard of strength adopted by British governments from 1887 onwards; and the great programmes of ship-building embodied in the Naval Defence Act of 1889, the Spencer programme of 1893, and the Goschen programme which followed, were frankly based on that consideration. There were times when the relative strength of the royal navy and of the allied fleets of France and Russia gave more reason for anxiety than any present or immediately prospective condition would justify.
Then, I propose to read a passage or two from the London 'Times'. For many weeks past, at any rate during the election in England, the London 'Times' has been publishing articles calculated as far as possible to alarm the people of England and to make them believe that the British government of to-day had not done and was not doing all that it ought to do and that there was a certain amount of peril in the preparations being made by Germany. I have here an article by a very able writer, written upon the occasion of the sixty-ninth birthday of Lord Fisher, who has recently passed out of the navy, and who, as everybody knows, was the first sea lord, for five years. I quote from the 'Times' of January 28, last.
Not an editorial?

No, it is not an editorial. But it is written by a

well known writer who is constantly writing military and defence articles for the 'Times':
The most striking, though, in our judgment, by no means the most important, achievement of Lord Fisher has been the introduction of the Dreadnought type of warship. Not much need be said upon this subject. It is full of technicalities little fitted for popular discussion, and it positively bristles with controversy. There are those who hold that the introduction of the Dreadnought type in 1905 was premature, that it was too hastily adopted-as is held to be shown by the large modifications introduced into the succeeding vessels of the same type both in this country and abroad-and that it has involved this country in a vast increase of naval expenditure which might have been postponed, if not avoided altogether. It would carry us too far into the kind of controversy which we desire to avoid on the present occasion to discuss these criticisms. The broad facts are indisputable-first, that all the great naval powers have now adopted the Dreadnought type with no greater modifications than time and experience have suggested to ourselves as well as to others; secondly, that the introduction of the type effected a marked pause in the development of the constructive programme of other powers; and, thirdly, that the duration of this pause gave this country a lead in the construction of Dreadnoughts which we still retain and can lose only by cur own craven default.

Any one who takes the trouble may, by consulting the navy list and other official documents accessible to all the world, institute for himself a comparison between the strength of the naval forces actually in commission in home waters at the end of 1904 and at the beginning of 1910. Who is the author?

The article is not signed, but I fancy it is written by Mr. Amery. We may accept it, I think, coming from the ' Times ' as a reliable authority, and this is a table which the ' Times ' would not publish if it had not verified the figures.
W'as not the person who wrote that article a Mr. Amery and who advocated those views, defeated at the last election?

I cannot tell what views he advocated; but I know the London ' Times ' did all it could to excite public opinion in England to the view that all was not being done that ought to be done for the navy, and that there was some danger from Germany. Now I propose to read some other authorities, and I intend to begin with the Prime Minister of England. On the 10th of November at the Lord Mayor's banquet, Mr. Asquith said:
When I addressed your predecessors in this place last year the internation sky here and in Europe was somewhat clouded and there were signs in the horizon which might well have seemed to foretell a spell of stormy weather.
I am happy to be able to speak to you to-niglit without any lurking apprehensions which it was then not wholly possible to lay aside.
My hon. friends ought to have introduced their resolution last March and got ahead of this trouble which the Prime Minister says existed about that time but fortunately had disappeared. He goes on:
If I speak for one moment of Germany, it is to say again that I know of nothing which need stand in the way of a full and friendly understanding which it is, I believe, a cherished object of the wisest statesmanship and of the best moral and social forces in both countries to promote.
That was at the Lord Mayor's banquet. And again on the 21st of December, Mr. Asquith said:
Let me say once for all that the navy is able to maintain not only now, but in future years, our supremacy at sea, and to guarantee the integrity of our shores, the protection of our commerce, and the inviolability of our empire. naval defence.
We are told that we can have responsible government in anything else, we can make our own game laws, we can administer our own affairs and even have control of our land forces, but on matters of naval defence we should have no power of our own.
Who made that statement? The British government, the British admiralty, any person in a responsible position in this House or in the country? My hon. friend knows that when he made that statement it was a complete fiction of imagination. But he went further; he did exactly the same with reference to autonomy, he did exactly the same with reference to centralization, and he did exactly the same with reference to taxation without representation. He trotted out the old ghosts of Baldwin and Lafontaine, overworked already by my right hon. friend. Will he ever give them a rest? is true. Responsible government is ours. That is true. But both the., autonomy and the responsible government have their orbits and apply in these orbits and in these orbits alone. When responsible government was granted to Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, or Ontario and Quebec, it was granted by the Crown, but it did not give' either of those provinces under the exercise of responsible government any claim to exercise for themselves the prerogatives of the Crown which were not included in the grant of responsible government. Autonomy, said my right hon. friend, was given to us, and when it was given to us, no bounds were set to it, and to-day it is free to inclose the whole world. Fine as a figure of speech, but utterly fallacious as a statement of principle or of law. Autonomy for your province and for our Dominion is autonomy with an orbit of its own, complete therein and legitimately opposing any that would gainsay or cross it within its own orbit; but the very moment that it goes further, it is no longer autonomy; it becomes something very different, it may become separation, independence, rebellion even. So, when my right hon. friend talks about centralization, there are some things in which it is sensible to centralize, and if there is any one thing on which competent opinion declares that it is sensible and economical and only safe to have centralization, it is the matter of defence of the empire. It takes at least six years to drill a boy to make him efficient for such service. Watch these divisions of the English fleet as they are perfecting themselves for war. How do they perfect themselves? By scrubbing clean and keeping polished the decks of their vessels? That is one thing. By turning out in clean and natty uniform? That is another thing.
