But to find out the secret of efficiency, consider the fleet when inky blackness envelops the sea, when all lights are out. and when every ship is in its place with its servers and satellites in their proper places, and, in the inky darkness going full steam ahead. That is where they get their training, that is where they perfect themselves to steal upon the enemy and strike first. Could you get anything like this out of these vessels that these gentlemen pretend to build? The natty uniform, the well-filled table, the drilling on deck, the manning of the guns to a certain extent-these things can be taught, but these vessels would no more be allowed to go in as a portion of the British fleet going into war than you, Sir, would be taken as the general of an army. And my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) agrees with that.
Now, I approach another subject. I propose to speak what I think. I have shown this House that, from the entrance of my right hon. friend into these conferences, commencing with 1902, on the question of defence, he has taken one position and one only, a position of absolute antagonism to any effective help of the British empire as a whole. I have followed the history of this branch of the navy which he proposes to build for Canada itself and have shown by his own expressions and those of his followers that it is to be built in Canada, kept in Canada and used for Canada and Canada alone-an utter negation of anything like contribution or help for imperial defence. And he says that, unless you can prove an emergency, you should not get anything else. I take exception there and then. I say that, if for nothing else but the almost intolerable burden which the British taxpayer has been carrying and is to-day carrying, and which will be made heavier upon him with each succeeding year, for which he and he alone pays, but as the result of which we have the security of our commerce, the security and peace of our country, the peace of the empire and the world;-I say that, for this Teason and, outside of all emergencies, Canada with her one hundred millions of revenue, with her strength and wealth and power, ought to contribute immediately toward that navy from which she has taken the benefits and Mr. FOSTER.
to which she has given nothing in men or money. Well, I am led to conclude that my Tight hon. friend has taken this stand from the old-time conviction personal to himself. I do not think you can separate a man from his whole political experience. In Australia no man on either side has piped up with this tune of ' invasion of responsible government ' or ' maintenance of autonomy.' No statesman on either side of the Australian House could be twitted with having spoken independence sentiments of having given utterance to any other sentiment than that of loyalty and fealty to the empire. Their men stand on the platform and in the House of parliament and declare that their fleet goes to the empire's support when the empire calls. Whatever order in council we have to pass, they say, whatever pro forma authority we have to give, these vessels shall go when the mother country needs them. If we had a government in Canada such as they have in Australia, we should have little doubts upon this matter. But, under the present government of Canada, led absolutely' as it is by one man, we have a right to ask ourselves something as to the past history and past public record of this gentleman.	.
And first I have a quarrel with my right hon. friend, this pink of a British .citizen, this example of an English Liberal, for doing what no British statesman, no English Liberal that I ever heard of, would do-going to a foreign country and animadverting unfavourably upon the conduct of his own country and of the motherland. Sir, in the city of Boston, over and over again, my right hon. friend, though he was under the oath of a privy councillor, stood before audiences and criticised the conduct of Canada and England in the civil war of the United States. And, in that troublous time, when we were asserting with courtesy and perfect fairness the rights of Canada to the waters that were given to her by the treaty of 1818, what did the right hon. gentleman say?
In the civil war the English people and the Canadian people did not show then the least sympathy.	.
England fitted out armed cruisers to prey upon and destroy American commerce.
We allowed American filibusters to raid Vermont and New York frontier towns.
Canada failed in her duty.
In my opinion the conduct of England, of Canada, towards the United States during the war was a disgrace to the civilization of England, of Canada. The American people could fight their own battles; they required no help, hut when they were engaged in a supreme struggle for the life or death of this great nation; when they were fighting for a cause as great, as holy, as ever engaged the devotion of men; when they had reason to expect the outspoken sympathy of those nearest to them, it was galling that southern privateers could be built, manned and equipped in England,

with the passive connivance of the British government, to destroy American commerce on the high seas; it was galling that rebel refugees could find shelter in Canada, and there, with impunity and without provoking condemnation, plot abominable crimes to help secession.
I find no fault with my right hon. friend for holding these sentiments if he so reads history. What I say is that you would search far and long to find a British statesman who would take such an occasion, before a people that were not over-friendly at that time, to call in question the acts of his country.
Well Sir, I have another thing to say with regard to my right hon. friend. His frantic attempts to tack Canada on to the United States in its fiscal policy, and in 1891, to drive the wedge of discrimination and of separation between the mother country and Canada in favour of the United States, does not show to my mind that he is very much in favour of British connection. 1891 has a history fore and aft. It was preceded by continental union and commercial union, in both of which my hon. friend participated, it was preceded by statements made in tin province of Quebec when my right hon. friend said of Mr. Mercier, ' Mr. Mercier is the greatest Canadian since the time of Papineau. I believe with Mr. Mercier, and I am here to make Mr. Mercier prevail.' And Mr. Mercier did prevail in 1890; then Mr. Mercier turned around in 1891, and he says to his people. ' I am fighting for the supremacy of Mr. Laurier my friend in the Dominion House. When we put. him there. Quebec will get all that she asks.' If there ever was a treaty entered into and publicly ratified, it was between Mr. Mercier and Mr. Wilfrid Laurier of that time. Now what happened in 1885? A memorable day was seen in the city of Montreal, and on the Champs de Mars, Mr. Mercier, and a gentleman by the name of Wilfrid Laurier, both spoke; and this gentleman by the name of Wilfrid Laurier, who was a sworn Privy Councillor at that excited period, and before that excited congregation declared that if he had been on the banks of the Saskatchewan he would have shouldered his musket and would have levelled it at the soldiers of the Queen. Immediately after that, two things took place. Mr. Mercier became an apostle of independence, and travelled the United States in 1892 and 1893, delivering hundreds of lectures, all in favour of the independence of Canada, declaring that only by being independent could we get our rights, amongst others the right to make treaties with such countries as we wished. He, (Mr. Mercier), was allied with men in the United States of America, he drew his salary from them, he paid his expenses out of their collections. He travelled the country, as I said, enlisting French Canadians, and men of other nationalities, prominent American citizens, all 'in favour of the independence of Canada; and along with it was the propagation of continental union, and the union of Canada with the United States. While this was going on, where was my right hon. friend? In Boston preaching the same doctrine in 1892; in the House of Commons preaching the same doctrine in 1891 and 1892, the doctrine of separation and independence. You have heard his words read,
I need not read them again. Mr. Mercier's cardinal doctrine was:	' What we want is
the power to make our own treaties.' He was outside parliament. My right hon. friend was inside parliament, and my right hon. friend was doing inside parliament what Mr. Mercier was doing outside parliament. In 1892 he advocated and tried to have passed by this House the following resolution :
It is expedient to obtain the necessary powers to enable Her Majesty the Queen through her representative, the Governor General of Canada, upon the advice of his ministers, to appoint an agent to negotiate commercial treaties with other British possessions or with foreign states, subject to the prior consent or subsequent approval of the parliament of Canada.
And the parliament of Canada alone. Now, I ask my right hon. friend, and I ask this House:	What would have happened
in .this country if my right hon. friend had been successful, and Canada had demanded and had obtained that power? There would have been no guarantee for the union of Canada with the empire for a single five years. It was a demand, not for autonomy, it was a demand for sovereignty, and a sovereignty which, if it were exercised, would make two nations where now there is the mother country and the Dominion under the mother country. They were working together, and in those ways. Well Sir, what more? We find that my friend, before confederation, was inoculated with this same virus. Here is what he wrote in 1866:
We (of the Papineau school) do not care a fig for the English colonies. When any change [DOT]whatsoever is proposed in our political or social institutions, we do not look to see whether this change will be of use to the English colonies or to any other neighbour; we think only of Lower Canada and the French race. What have we in common with the English colonies? What interest, what relations bind us to them? Is it a matter of origin, religion, language, national aspirations? No, not at all.
In 1888 in the House of Commons he says:
The time is coming when the present relations between Great Britain and Canada

must either become closer or be severed altogether.
At the Club National, on the 2nd of July, 1890, he made another profession of faith:
I do not mean to say that we should always remain a colony; on the contrary, the day is coming when this country will have to take its place among the nations of the earth. But I do not want to see my country's independence attained through the hostility of one race to another.
That was directed against the attempt to form the Parti National.
I do not want my country's independence to be conceived in the blood of civil war. I want my country's independence to be reached through the normal and regular process of all the elements of its population towards the realization of a common aspiration.
JVell Sir, when we come down to 1892 he says:
I hold out to my fellow countrymen the idea of independence. But whenever the day comes it must come by the consent of both countries, and we shall continue to keep the good feeling and the good will of the mother land.
If we are true to our record we will again exhibit to the world the unique and unprecedented example of a nation achieving its independence by slow degrees and as naturally as the severing of the ripe fruit from the parent tree	I have again and again repeated that the goal of my aspiration is the independence of Canada, to see Canada an independent nation, in due course of time.
These were not the outpourings of a youthful and immature imagination, these were the studied statements of an old and seasoned public man, uttered in Boston, and repeated in the House of Commons of Canada, and up to this day my right hon. friend has not disavowed that that is still his goal. I invite him to do so now.
He will not do it, he still maintains that opinion; that is still his goal. We can quite well see why in 1902, in 1907, in 1909, and now in 1910, he refuses absolutely to link up with the British empire, he declines absolutely to do anything else than to build what he builds in Canada for Canada, and to be used alone in Canada, with the exception of words-and of words my right hon. friend is prodigal. He makes his declaration that that is his settled policy, settled in 1902, settled to this day; yet on the face of it, he declares that the supremacy of the British empire is necessary to the security of this country, as well as to every other part of the empire. He declares that it is the only security for the commerce and the peace and prosperity of the British empire and the peace of the world. These are his words; those that I have been describing are words plus deeds and deeds in the tenor and line of the words,

And to-night, when I put his record before him and challenge him as to whether or not as Prime Minister of this country, leading the foremost Dominion in this empire of ours, he still adheres to his statement of doctrine, over and over made, that he believes and cherishes as his goal the independence of this country and a severing of the ties that bind us to the old land, I think this House and I think this country will come to its own conclusion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

But that is not all. My
right hon. friend has never missed an op-portuntiy of belittling and deriding the diplomacy of the British empire, never.
Is there a Canadian anywhere who would not hail with joy the day when we would be deprived of the services of British diplomacy?
Mr. right hon. friend is responsible for that statement.
\\ hat has been British diplomacy to us, Sir? British diplomacy, so far as Canada is concerned, has been a I'ecord of failure, of surrender, and of sacrifice.
Up and down this country he has preached that doctrine. Why? To lessen the respect of a British country for its home country and its home government, to instill the insidious poison into the minds of young and growing citizens that the old country does not know what it is doing and has not treated us fairly. To-night, Sir, I cannot go into the matter of the record of British diplomacy, but I am willing to dp it at any time, and I have not much use, I say it straight, I have not much use for a public man representing the highest position in this country who finds nothing better to do than to go up and down this country deriding and misrepresenting British diplomacy and wishing for the day when we may be rid of it. My right hon. friend will not deny that.
But he has done more than that. He has never given up an opportunity, during the last 10 or 15 years, of representing Canada as engaged in deadly conflict, wrenching from the British government tyrannical government, rights and privileges, and he has stretched to the very verge of a very vivid imagination the rights and privileges which we to-day enjoy by virtue of the concessions of the British prerogative. And so his Minister of Marine afterwards comes back from the conference of 1909 and says: We have wrenched from Great Britain our political autonomy, we have wrenched from Great Britain our treaty-making autonomy, we have wrenched from Great Britain our fiscal autonomy, and now I come back with our naval autonomy. All these things my rieht hon. friend speaks, lesser men echo

what he says. These are but the results of teaching. The Postmaster General said the other day that a bad canvass was being used against the government in Quebec, that the government were represented as sacrificing on the altar of Moloch the youth and vigour of the country for the sake of European wars. I think I am not misrepresenting my hon. friend. My hon. friend knows the story of old, about the one who ploughed the furrow and who sowed the dragon's teeth therein and found himself straightway confronted by armed men. These are the armed men which were sown by my right hon. friend and his colleagues in 1896 and later. Don't I know it, don't I know that the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. L. P. Brodeur), and Mr. Monet, since translated to his reward, and sundry others, went up and down the lines in the province of Quebec and represented to audience after audience that we had actually made a grant to get rifles for our soldiers and artillery for our troops, and that the babes were to be torn from the mothers' breasts, and the lovers to be torn from their sweethearts' arms and carried away to be sacrificed in this vortex of militarism? It was all very nice to erect Moloch's altars then and sacrifice on them, but the armed men have sprung up and thev aTe confronting my right hon. friend and his lieutenants at this very moment.
But what more, Sir. Not only that, hut then comes this last straw which breaks the camel's back. We have a good old song which often we have sung, thousands of throats have sung it throughout the length and breadth of the empire and de-liehted to do it:	God Save Our King.
But, now, we have got to substitute another word, and hereafter our song will be: God save our suzerain, long live our suzerain, God bless the suzerain. That may be a light thing for my right hon. friend, but it is exactly in line with every other effort to weaken the respect for sovereignty and the respect for the ties that bind us to the old land. Are these things of little moment coming from a man of high degree and of high place? I do not think so. This country is filling up with men who are foreign to our institutions and who have to be taught to become good British subjects. Is this the way to teach them? I do not think so. This may be a little thing to my right hon. friend, but is one of the things which in unison with the others shows the trend. Now, my deduction from all this is simply: If in Australia and New Zealand there is no unrest in the public mind, that when war time comes their fleets will go to the defence of the empire, it is because they have not been blessed with public men who have given utterance to diverse sentiments such as these I have been quoting. In 1899, this
country knows what took place. It knows that the deliberate intention of my right hon. friend was to prevent a single Canadian being sent to South Africa. We were the laggards, and if it had not been for the power of public opinion outside we would have been so far laggard that we would never have been in the race at all. I listened the other night to the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Fowke) in his desire to Lincolnize the head of the government, and I asked myself what in the world is he after that he puts it on so thick and so often. My hon. friend from South Ontario in comparing the Prime Minister to Lincoln, said that all the progress of this country in all its great epochs was due to the policy and the effort of my right hon. friend.
Quite correct.

Quite correct says the hon. gentleman. Now, to this eminently sane and sound and unprejudiced hearer, let me invite the consideration of four dates. There is the date of 1878, there is the date of 1882, there is the date of 1891, and there is the date of 1899.
And there is the date of 1896.

I never have treated my hon. friend (Mr. Talbot) who has just interrupted me as being a serious subject; he is so good natured and has been so often through the composing room that I will not lose time dealing with him.
1878 saw the institution of the industrial life of this country under the influence of protection, which alone brought into existence and kept in its development to 1896. In 1878 where was my right hon. friend and the Liberal party? If they had had their way in 1878 would you have had industrial Canada as it is to-day? That is one epoch. The other date is 1882. In 1882 the splendid project of uniting this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific with a great transcontinental railway was launched, and it took stress and strain and money hardly to be got to carry it through. Does anybody dispute the proposition that the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway and its work has been one of the prime elements in the progress of Canada? Where would that railroad have been if my right hon. friend and his party had had their way?
In 1891 it was a struggle, life and death, 'for the perpetuation of British connection in this country. There is no doubt about it. My right hon. friend laughs at British connection. Edward Blake was a man intellectually far superior to my right hon. friend. He had so much imagination, he was not gifted with so

much levity of thought, he did not depend so much on airy rhetoric, but Edward Blake had a brain of tremendous power; Edward Blake was loyal. And when the 1891 propaganda of the right hon. gentleman was driven to its conclusion, Edward Blake left him and his reasons for leaving are on record to this date. He left the right hon. gentleman, because, he said, that if the right hon. gentleman's policy were to be successful it would end in severing the bonds that bound Canada to the empire. And, that the right hon. gentleman was not successful was due to the work of the Liberal Conservative party. The last date is 1899, and what happened in 1899? The Boer war broke out. The other colonies jumped into the field, the governments trying to keep ahead of their people and the people trying to run close to their governments. There was no schism between them. But in Canada the constitutional bogey was put up. Parliamentary sanction was invoked. There was no power to do this and do that, and if my right hon. friend had his way not a Canadian would have been sent to South Africa. Now, Sir, I hold that taken by and large, no one event that ever happened in the Dominion of Canada has done so much to elevate Canada in the plane of action, to widen its horizon and win it greater place and prominence in the wide world than resulted from Canadian volunteers going to South Africa and fighting as they fought on the plains of Africa for the old flag. For many a long distant day Canada will not cease to find the beneficial effects accruing to her from our part in that transaction. And, Sir, if my right hon. friend had had his way that would never have happened. Therefore, these four dates may well be conned over by hon. gentlemen and may well be thought out by the people of this Dominion. Now, Mr. Speaker, I have spoken longer than I intended.
Go on.
I have other things I would like to say.
Adjourn the debate.

Before moving the adjournment of this debate, I think that the remarkable speech which has fallen from the hon. gentleman who has just sat down (Mr. Foster) deserves a word or two of comment from hon. gentlemen on this side. I want to say a few words regarding the unique position he occupies to-night. I have heard him on numerous occasions since I have had the honour of a seat in this House, but rarely have I seen him in a more desperate frame of mind. After having been compelled to eat every word he said a year ago, when, with all the adjectives and invectives he had at his hand he declared that it would be unwise and improper thing for Canada to give a contribution, and that the proper thing for her was to build her own navy,-after he had been compelled to do this by the men who supply the sinews of war during election times and who applied the thumb screw and the composing room to himself and his leader in order to make them withdraw from the position they had taken -after he and his leader had performed a feat, the like of which has only been heard of in history once before when ' the King of France with twice ten thousand men marced up the hill and then marched down again,' the hon. gentleman sought to cover his disgraceful retreat by endeavouring to discredit the right hon. gentleman who has guided the destinies of Canada so success-fullv since the Liberal party took office in 1896. If I wanted to go into ancient history, I could tell some home truths about the man who was premier of this country and leader of the Conservative party and who declared himself in favour of annexation, I could bring into prominence again the Pacific scandal and the notorious nest of traitors and moments of weakness, but I shall not be lead away by the example of the hon. gentleman. I say that it was undignified and unbecoming for a gen-

tleman occupying the position the hon. gentleman does, to talk as he did about the man who governs this country and whom every Liberal in Canada is proud to follow-to talk about his being an enemy of the empire and a separatist. Why, the fourteen years of his administration is a sufficient answer to the slander. What record has the hon. gentleman to show? When he was Minister of Finance did it ever enter into his head that Canada should show some slight appreciation of England's great watchfulness over her by giving a preference in the Canadian market? No, that was left for the Liberal leader to do. When there was a war in the Soudan, what course did the Tory government, of which my hon. friend was then Finance Minister, take? They said to the English government: We will allow you to enlist our young men in this country, but we will not give you a dollar. And yet this hon. gentleman talks about his party having forced Sir Wilfrid Laurier to send Canadian troops to South Africa. Sir, we all know it was left to a French Canadian, at the head of the Canadian government, to see that Canadians, for the first time in the history of this country, were sent by their government to fight the battles of the empire.
Let me give you an evidence of the opinion in which the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is held in England. You have all heard of Mr. Richard Jebb, the gentleman who ran as a Liberal Unionist in St. Pancras and whom the imperial federationists of this country asked Mr. Balfour to select as a candidate. Well, Mr. Jebb says, in his ' Sketches of colonial nationalism,' speaking of the Prime Minister of Canada:
Reviewing the events which have taken place since the passing of the Transvaal resolution by the Dominion parliament in the summer of 1899, Canadians, after all, have no reason to think that their country has failed to keep her accustomed lead in the steady movement towards imperial co-operation. On the contrary, in the end as at the beginning, Canada figures as the resolute guardian when others were tempted to turn aside of that mutual independence which is the sure foundation of imperial union. Prominent amongst nationalist statesmen stands Sir Wilfrid Laurier successfully applying to the constructive problem of the empire the fearless and progressive spirit of this political tradition.
When Mr. Jebb, with his record on imperial subjects gives that certificate of character to the leader of the Liberal party in Canada, my right hon. friend need not care about what the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) says. One remark more before I move the adjournment. When listening to the hon. member (Mr. Foster) talking about the motherland and what Canada
. Mr. MACDONALD.
owed the empire, I asked myself whether his judgment would be as good as that of a young man, a son of Nova Scotia, who led the Nova Scotians at Paardeberg, who wears the decoration of Her Majesty for the distinction he won in fighting the battles of the empire in South Africa. Would not the judgment of such a man be worth far more than that of the hon. gentleman who has used up the time of this House for purely partisan purposes? To-night I received this letter from the young gentleman in question, whose devotion and patriotism cannot be gainsaid :
Dear Mr. Macdonald,-Canadian attitude on the naval question being in the forefront, I hope you will not think me presuming upon your time and patience if I venture to place before you the situation as it appears to one who is not in the active political field.
The first thing to be settled is to find out at what objects we are aiming.
It seems to me that the only contribution truly acceptable to the Canadian mind must be in the form of Canadian flesh and blood, that is to say in trained Canadian seamen. If Canada is to pay Englishmen to do Canada's share of the fighting, we had better step down and out.
Our immediate object should be to commence the training of a body of, say 2,000 Canadian sailors. These men can be drawn from inland cities and counties of Canada just as well as from the maritime ports, because the crew of a modern warship are not so much sailors in the usual sense of the word as they are artillervmen, riflemen, mechanics and engineers of all kinds, and the inland cities and towns can furnish their quota just as well as the maritime provinces.
The reason that the South African War was of such vital interest to Canada, was because she had some 8,000 men there, all of them writing home, and every city, town, county and street in Canada could say that it had a representative fighting in South Africa.
Had the contribution of Canada in the South African War taken the form of a cash contribution or the contribution of magnificent batteries of inanimate guns, Canada's enthusiasm would have been insignificant.
Canada's proper contribution to imperial defence must be in trained Canadian men, and to train these men we must commence a navy.
If war should be declared to-morrow, a contribution of $10,000,000 or five times that amount, if you like, can be voted by the Canadian parliament and placed at England's disposal.
Outside of all this there is the constitutional question, and the Liberal government deserve the thanks and the everlasting gratitude of every member of the British empire in its refusal to be stampeded into committing a false step in our imperial relations.
The surest and quickest way to an effective form of imperial union is the maintenance by Canada of a dignified attitude, and there is no occasion for us to lapse into the colonial position which our ancesters did so much to extricate us from.

If the process of giving Dreadnoughts is commenced the English people will expect a continuation of such policy, and its discontinuance will cause more friction than ever exists at present.
I entirely disapprove of any action which will lead to condition of affairs from which Canada will find it difficult to withdraw, and have not the slightest hesitation in saying that Sir Wilfrid Laurier's policy is merely a logical step in the process of colonial and imperial development at which we have heen busy for so many years.
The surest aid which Canada can give to the development of the empire is the establishment qi a robust Canadianism, able to place in the fighting line of the empire trained Canadian seamen as it has already placed trained Canadian soldiers.
And, after all this long harangue in which my hon. friend descended to the old game of abusing those who did not agree with him-because he had a poor case- and before moving the adjournment of the debate, I wanted to give the opinion of Richard Jebb, the imperialist, as to the estimation in which Sir Wilfrid Laurier is held in England-aye, and wherever the English language is spoken; and I wanted to give the answer from a man who knows- a man who went out and fought the battles of the empire, not one who stayed at home and dotted 'i's' ^nd crossed 'tV and twisted words and distorted ideas. These are an answer sufficient for to-night to the address of my hon. friend, and so I move the adjournment of the debate.

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow?

speechtext: To-morrow is Friday and it is not likelv that we shall have a full House. We will not take up this debate, but will go on with estimates.
What estimates?
